title: Tongues of fire (Acts 2:1–13)
hookLine: Parthians, Medes, Elamites: the list of nations who heard
tomorrow: the man who denied him by a fire stands up to speak. what does he say?

lines: YOUR LANGUAGE, WHERE YOU DIDN'T EXPECT IT.
cards: Hearing your own language where you didn't expect it lands differently: a cashier who switches to it, a song from a stranger's speaker, your grandmother's word for something. That's what happens at Pentecost.

The friends are "all with one accord in one place." A sound like wind fills the house, they begin to speak, and the crowd outside, gathered from everywhere, finds that "every man heard them speak in his own language."

teach.b: Acts sets the scene with sound and sight. "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting."
Then "cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." Each of them, not only the leaders.

The crowd is devout Jews staying in Jerusalem, out of every nation, and Acts names them like a roll call: Parthians, Medes and Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Egypt, Libya and Rome, Cretes and Arabians.

They can hardly take it in: "Behold, are not all these which speak Galilaeans? And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Wherein we were born: a mother tongue. Here's the surprise.
The miracle doesn't make everyone speak one language.
The many languages stay, and the same news arrives inside each of them: "the wonderful works of God."
Some readers hear an answer to the tower of Babel in Genesis, where one language scattered into many. At Pentecost the many aren't erased; they're understood.

One to tell a friend tonight: on the day some call the church's birthday, nobody had to change their accent to be included. Not everyone is moved, and Acts keeps both reactions. Some ask, "What meaneth this?"
Others laugh: "These men are full of new wine."

how: Christians celebrate Pentecost in the Easter season; some churches read Acts 2 aloud in several languages that day, and some wear red for the fire.

o: a fiery sermon preached out in the street
angry words that burn whoever hears them
flames on each of them as the Spirit came

p: the sound that filled the house
cloven tongues like as of fire
devout Jews out of every nation

s: at Pentecost everyone began speaking one shared language
the opposite: every man heard them speak in his own language.
the crowd asked how they heard Galileans in their own native tongues

games.q: at your cousin's wedding, the groom's grandparents speak only Korean. you know one phrase. what fits Pentecost?
o: say the one phrase you know, warmly, and ask them for another.
stay quiet, so you don't get it wrong in front of them.
speak English slowly; they'll pick up the meaning.
games.why: at Pentecost the languages weren't erased; each heard in his own. a few words in someone's mother tongue say you came to them.

practice: Say hello out loud in three languages: your own, one from your family's story or your street, and one you've only heard. Say each one slowly, the way you'd want someone to say your grandmother's word.
With each, hold in mind a face that would light up hearing it.

wordCard.voice: Tongues of fire. The flames that sat on each of them at Pentecost, and the many languages that came after.

orig.note: Greek: tongue, and also language. Acts 2:3–4 uses it for the flames and for the speaking.

carryVoice: Here's the line: each in his own language, and nobody had to change accents to belong. Day three in Acts.
